lessons.title: Iron Absorption, Transport & Hepcidin Regulation

levels.kid:
Iron is a tiny metal your body needs to build red blood cells. Red cells use iron to grab oxygen and carry it all around your body.

You get iron from foods like meat, beans and spinach. It gets into your body through your gut, mostly at the very start of the small intestine.

Then a delivery truck called **transferrin** carries the iron through your blood to the places that need it.

Here is the clever part. Your body has almost no way to get rid of extra iron, so it controls how much comes in. A hormone called **hepcidin**, made by the liver, works like a gatekeeper. When you have plenty of iron, hepcidin closes the gate. When you need more, the gate opens.

Most iron is also reused from old red cells, like building with recycled blocks.
levels.hs:
**Iron** is the metal at the center of **hemoglobin**, the protein that lets red blood cells carry oxygen. An adult body holds about 3 to 4 grams of iron, and roughly two-thirds of it sits inside hemoglobin.

Key facts:
- **Recycling is the main supply.** Every day, cells called **macrophages** (mostly in the spleen) eat old red cells and return their iron to the blood. This provides most of the iron used to make new hemoglobin.
- **Absorption is small.** The gut takes in only about 1 to 2 milligrams of iron a day, just enough to replace what is lost.
- **There is no off switch for losing iron.** The body loses iron only passively, through shed skin and gut cells and small blood losses. So the only way to control iron levels is to control how much is absorbed.

Iron is absorbed in the **duodenum**, the first part of the small intestine. **Heme iron** from meat is absorbed more easily than **nonheme iron** from plants. Vitamin C helps nonheme iron absorption; tea, calcium and phytates in grains reduce it.

Iron leaves gut cells through a doorway protein called **ferroportin**. In the blood it rides on **transferrin**, and extra iron is stored inside cells in a protein called **ferritin**.

The master controller is **hepcidin**, a hormone made by the liver. Hepcidin rises when iron is plentiful and shuts the ferroportin doorway. Example: after someone donates blood, their hepcidin falls, so they absorb more iron to rebuild red cells.
levels.college:
Iron is essential but toxic when free, because ferrous iron (Fe2+) catalyzes the formation of damaging hydroxyl radicals. Iron handling is therefore built around carrier proteins and tight control of entry.

**Absorption in the duodenal enterocyte:**
- Dietary nonheme iron is mostly ferric (Fe3+). The brush-border enzyme **DCYTB** (duodenal cytochrome b) reduces it to Fe2+.
- **DMT1** (divalent metal transporter 1) imports Fe2+, coupled to protons; gastric acid helps keep iron soluble.
- Heme is taken up by a still-uncertain mechanism, then **heme oxygenase** releases the iron inside the cell.
- Iron inside the enterocyte is either stored in **ferritin** (lost when the cell is shed after a few days) or exported.

**Export and transport:**
- **Ferroportin** is the only known cellular iron exporter. It works with **hephaestin**, a ferroxidase that converts Fe2+ back to Fe3+. Macrophages and liver cells use the plasma ferroxidase **ceruloplasmin** instead.
- **Transferrin** binds two Fe3+ ions. Normal transferrin saturation is roughly 20 to 45%.
- Developing red cells take up transferrin through **transferrin receptor 1 (TfR1)** by endocytosis. The endosome acidifies, iron is released, and transferrin and its receptor recycle to the surface.

**Hepcidin**, a 25-amino-acid peptide hormone from hepatocytes, binds ferroportin and causes its internalization and degradation. High hepcidin traps iron in enterocytes and macrophages, so plasma iron falls. Hepcidin is:
- **Raised** by high iron stores and by inflammation, mainly via the cytokine **IL-6**.
- **Lowered** by iron deficiency, hypoxia and increased red cell production. Erythroblasts stimulated by erythropoietin release **erythroferrone**, which suppresses hepcidin.

**Cellular control** uses **iron regulatory proteins (IRPs)**. When a cell is iron-poor, IRPs bind iron-responsive elements on mRNAs: they block translation of ferritin (less storage) and stabilize TfR1 mRNA (more uptake).
levels.phd:
Systemic iron homeostasis is an endocrine circuit: hepcidin (encoded by **HAMP**) sets plasma iron by controlling ferroportin (SLC40A1). Hepcidin was identified in 2000 to 2001 as an antimicrobial peptide (Krause; Park, Ganz and colleagues), and Nicolas et al. linked it to iron when mice lacking it, through disruption of the neighbouring Usf2 gene, developed iron overload. Nemeth et al. (Science 2004) showed hepcidin binding triggers ferroportin ubiquitination, endocytosis and lysosomal degradation. Cryo-EM (Billesbolle et al., 2020) showed hepcidin also occludes the ferroportin central cavity, with binding enhanced when iron occupies the transporter, a second mechanism that blocks export directly.

**Transcriptional control of HAMP:**
- **BMP-SMAD axis.** Liver sinusoidal endothelial cells secrete **BMP6** (rising with liver iron) and BMP2. These bind BMP receptors with the coreceptor **hemojuvelin (HJV)**, phosphorylating SMAD1/5/8, which partner with SMAD4 to drive HAMP.
- **Transferrin sensing.** As holo-transferrin rises, it displaces **HFE** from TfR1, freeing HFE to interact with **TfR2** and enhance BMP signaling.
- **TMPRSS6** (matriptase-2) cleaves HJV and dampens signaling. Loss-of-function mutations cause inappropriately high hepcidin and iron-refractory iron deficiency anemia (IRIDA).
- **Inflammation:** IL-6 activates JAK-STAT3 at the HAMP promoter; activin B contributes via SMAD signaling.
- **Erythroid suppression:** Kautz et al. (2014) identified **erythroferrone (ERFE)**. ERFE-knockout mice showed delayed hepcidin suppression after phlebotomy and slower recovery from anemia. ERFE acts as a ligand trap for BMP6 and related BMPs.

**Cellular regulation.** IRP1 (a bifunctional cytosolic aconitase that loses its 4Fe-4S cluster when iron is low) and IRP2 (degraded by FBXL5 when iron is replete) bind 5' IREs to repress ferritin and ferroportin translation, and 3' IREs to stabilize TfR1 mRNA. Duodenal enterocytes and erythroid precursors express an alternative ferroportin transcript (FPN1B) lacking the 5' IRE (Zhang et al., 2009), allowing export to continue during iron deficiency. Enterocyte **HIF-2alpha** upregulates DCYTB, DMT1 and ferroportin when iron or oxygen is low. Ferritin iron is mobilized by **NCOA4**-mediated ferritinophagy.

A notable controversy: HCP1 was proposed as the intestinal heme importer, but it proved to be mainly the proton-coupled folate transporter (PCFT), and heme uptake remains incompletely defined.
levels.expert:
Translating hepcidin biology into practice raises several points that go beyond the core pathway.

**Measuring hepcidin.** Assays (mass spectrometry and immunoassays) were long unharmonized, so absolute values differ between labs. Levels show diurnal variation and rise in chronic kidney disease partly through reduced renal clearance. Hepcidin is mainly a research and specialist tool, not a routine test.

**Oral iron and the hepcidin rebound.** Isotope studies by Moretti, Stoffel and colleagues (2015 to 2017) showed that oral iron itself raises hepcidin for roughly a day, lowering fractional absorption from the next intake. This supported alternate-day schedules in iron-deficient women, a shift in how guidelines think about oral repletion.

**Nutritional immunity.** Hepcidin-driven hypoferremia withholds iron from siderophilic pathogens. Arezes et al. (2015) showed hepcidin-deficient mice are highly vulnerable to Vibrio vulnificus, and a hepcidin agonist was protective. High transferrin saturation produces non-transferrin-bound iron (NTBI), which is especially available to microbes and taken up by tissues without regulation.

**Therapeutics targeting the axis:**
- Raising hepcidin activity restricts iron to erythropoiesis. **Rusfertide**, a hepcidin mimetic, reduced phlebotomy needs in polycythemia vera in the phase 3 VERIFY trial (2025). Minihepcidins, the oral ferroportin inhibitor **vamifeport**, and TMPRSS6-silencing siRNA or antisense drugs are being studied in beta-thalassemia and polycythemia vera.
- Lowering hepcidin aims to release sequestered iron. Anti-hemojuvelin antibodies are in trials, and HIF prolyl hydroxylase inhibitors used for anemia of chronic kidney disease lower hepcidin indirectly through erythropoietic signaling.

**Physiology to remember.** Hepcidin is suppressed in later pregnancy, which boosts maternal absorption for fetal iron transfer.

**Neurosurgical angle.** Brain iron enters through TfR1 on blood-brain barrier endothelium. After intracerebral hemorrhage, heme iron released from lysed red cells drives oxidative injury and ferroptosis. Yet the i-DEF trial (2019) found deferoxamine futile for improving good functional outcome at 90 days, a reminder that compelling iron biology does not guarantee clinical benefit.

**Open questions** include exactly how hepatocytes sense holo-transferrin, how dietary heme is imported, and whether brain iron is regulated by its own local hepcidin-ferroportin control.

Iron is absorbed in the duodenum via DCYTB and DMT1, then exported by ferroportin
Transferrin carries iron in plasma; ferritin stores it inside cells
The body has no regulated iron excretion, so absorption is the control point
Liver hepcidin degrades ferroportin: raised by iron and IL-6, lowered by erythroferrone and hypoxia
IRPs bind IREs to adjust ferritin and TfR1 in each cell

test.q: Where is most dietary iron absorbed?
test.explain: The duodenum, the first part of the small intestine, is the main site of iron absorption. The terminal ileum is where vitamin B12 is absorbed.

test.q: Which protein carries iron in the blood plasma?
test.explain: Transferrin binds two ferric iron ions and delivers them to cells. Ferritin stores iron inside cells, and ceruloplasmin is a copper-containing ferroxidase.

test.q: How does hepcidin lower plasma iron?
choices: Blocking DMT1 at the gut surface
test.explain: Hepcidin binds the iron exporter ferroportin and causes its internalization and degradation, trapping iron inside gut cells and macrophages.

test.q: Which organ produces hepcidin?
test.explain: Hepcidin is made by hepatocytes in the liver. The kidney makes erythropoietin, a different hormone.

test.q: Which enzyme on the duodenal brush border reduces ferric iron (Fe3+) to ferrous iron (Fe2+)?
test.explain: DCYTB reduces Fe3+ so DMT1 can import it. Hephaestin and ceruloplasmin do the opposite, oxidizing Fe2+ to Fe3+.

test.q: After blood loss, red cell production speeds up. What happens to hepcidin?
choices: It rises, so more iron is absorbed
It falls, so less iron is absorbed
It falls, so more iron is absorbed
It rises, so less iron is absorbed
test.explain: Stimulated erythroblasts release erythroferrone, which suppresses hepcidin. Ferroportin stays active, so more iron is absorbed and released from stores.

test.q: How does the body mainly lose iron?
choices: Shed cells and small blood losses
Sweat glands that pump out excess iron
test.explain: Iron loss is passive, through shed skin and gut cells and minor bleeding. There is no regulated excretion route, so absorption is the control point.

test.q: Most of the iron used each day for making hemoglobin comes from:
choices: Dietary iron absorbed in the gut
test.explain: Macrophages break down old red cells and return their iron to the blood. Daily gut absorption is small and mainly replaces losses.

test.q: Which dietary factor enhances absorption of nonheme iron?
test.explain: Vitamin C helps keep iron in the absorbable ferrous form. Calcium, tea polyphenols and phytates all reduce nonheme iron absorption.

test.q: Name the only known protein that exports iron out of cells.
test.explain: Ferroportin exports iron from enterocytes, macrophages and liver cells, and it is the target of hepcidin.

test.q: Inflammation raises hepcidin mainly through the cytokine ___.
test.explain: IL-6 activates JAK-STAT3 signaling at the hepcidin gene promoter, which drives hepcidin up during inflammation.

test.q: Which hormone released by erythroblasts suppresses hepcidin?
test.explain: Erythroferrone, released by erythroblasts stimulated by erythropoietin, lowers hepcidin so more iron reaches the marrow.

choices: To help your skin make sweat
To help your bones grow longer
kidTest.explain: Red blood cells use iron to grab oxygen and carry it around your body.

kidTest.q: Where does iron from food get into your body?
kidTest.explain: Iron gets in through the gut, mostly at the start of the small intestine.

kidTest.q: When your body already has plenty of iron, what does hepcidin do?
kidTest.explain: Hepcidin is the gatekeeper. With plenty of iron, it closes the gate so less comes in.

kidTest.q: Where does your body get most of its iron for new red cells?
kidTest.explain: The body recycles iron from old red cells, like reusing building blocks.

kidTest.q: The blood's iron delivery truck is called t _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Transferrin carries iron through the blood to the places that need it.

advancedTest.q: A patient has loss-of-function mutations in TMPRSS6. Which profile best fits?
advancedTest.explain: TMPRSS6 normally cleaves hemojuvelin to dampen BMP-SMAD signaling. Without it, hepcidin stays high, ferroportin is degraded, and iron-refractory iron deficiency anemia results.

advancedTest.q: In iron deficiency, IRPs repress translation of IRE-containing ferroportin mRNA. How do duodenal enterocytes still export iron?
choices: An alternative transcript lacks the IRE
Ferritin mRNA competes the IRPs away
IRP2 is degraded when iron is scarce
advancedTest.explain: Enterocytes express the FPN1B transcript, which lacks the 5' IRE and escapes IRP repression. IRP2 is degraded when iron is replete, not scarce.

advancedTest.q: What is the physiological rationale for alternate-day oral iron schedules?
choices: Each intake depletes DCYTB from the brush border
Each intake suppresses erythroferrone for a week
Each intake raises hepcidin, lowering next-day uptake
Each intake saturates transferrin for several days
advancedTest.explain: Isotope studies showed oral iron raises hepcidin for about a day, reducing fractional absorption from the next intake. Spacing intakes lets hepcidin fall back first.

advancedTest.q: Erythroferrone-knockout mice undergo phlebotomy. Based on Kautz et al. (2014), what is expected?
choices: No change, because BMP6 compensates at once
Delayed fall in hepcidin and slower recovery
Faster fall in hepcidin and quicker recovery
Rising hepcidin that leads to iron overload
advancedTest.explain: Without erythroferrone to trap BMPs, hepcidin is not promptly suppressed after blood loss, so iron supply to the marrow lags and recovery from anemia is delayed.

lessons.title: Iron Deficiency Anemia: Causes & Iron Studies

levels.kid:
Your red blood cells are like tiny delivery trucks that carry oxygen to every part of your body. To grab oxygen, each truck needs **iron**. Without enough iron, the body makes fewer trucks, and the ones it makes come out small and pale.

This is called **iron deficiency anemia**. A person might feel very tired, look pale, or get out of breath climbing stairs. Some people even crave chewing ice!

Iron can run low for a few reasons:
- Eating too few iron-rich foods like red meat, beans and spinach.
- Growing very fast, so the body needs extra.
- Losing blood, because blood is full of iron.

Doctors check a blood test called **ferritin**. Ferritin is like a storage box for iron. A low number means the box is nearly empty.
levels.hs:
**Anemia** means too little **hemoglobin**, the iron-containing protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen. Each hemoglobin molecule holds four iron atoms, so when iron runs short the bone marrow cannot build enough of it. **Iron deficiency anemia (IDA)** is the most common anemia in the world.

Iron runs low for three main reasons:
- **Blood loss**, the biggest cause in adults: heavy menstrual periods, or slow bleeding from the stomach or intestines.
- **Higher demand**: pregnancy, infancy and growth spurts in teenagers.
- **Poor intake or absorption**: diets low in iron, or gut diseases like celiac disease that damage the part of the intestine that absorbs iron.

Symptoms include tiredness, pale skin, shortness of breath, and odd cravings for ice or dirt (called **pica**).

Doctors diagnose IDA with **iron studies**:
- **Ferritin**: reflects stored iron. Low ferritin is the most specific sign.
- **Serum iron**: iron in the blood right now. Low.
- **TIBC** (total iron-binding capacity): how much iron the blood's transport protein, **transferrin**, could carry. High, because the body makes more transferrin when hungry for iron.
- **Transferrin saturation**: how full transferrin is. Low.

Example: a 16-year-old with heavy periods feels exhausted at soccer practice. Her red cells are small and pale, and her ferritin is very low. Treating the iron deficiency, and the heavy bleeding, restores her energy.
levels.college:
Iron deficiency develops in **stages**, which explains why some tests turn abnormal before others:
- **Iron depletion**: stores fall, so **ferritin** drops, but hemoglobin is normal.
- **Iron-deficient erythropoiesis**: stores are exhausted; **transferrin saturation** falls and transferrin (measured as **TIBC**) rises. Hemoglobin may still be normal.
- **Iron deficiency anemia**: hemoglobin falls and cells become **microcytic** (low MCV) and **hypochromic** (low MCH).

**Causes** by mechanism:
- **Loss**: menstrual bleeding (the leading cause in premenopausal women), gastrointestinal bleeding from ulcers, NSAID use, angiodysplasia or colorectal cancer, frequent blood donation, and hookworm infection worldwide.
- **Demand**: pregnancy, infancy, adolescence.
- **Absorption**: iron is absorbed mainly in the duodenum and needs stomach acid to stay soluble. Celiac disease, *H. pylori* gastritis, autoimmune atrophic gastritis, bariatric bypass surgery and long-term acid suppression all impair it.

**Classic iron-study pattern**: low ferritin, low serum iron, high TIBC, low transferrin saturation. Ferritin below about 30 ng/mL strongly suggests deficiency; below 15 ng/mL is nearly diagnostic.

**Blood count and smear**: low MCV, high **RDW** (cells vary in size as new small cells mix with old normal ones), elongated **pencil cells**, and often reactive thrombocytosis.

**IDA vs thalassemia trait**: both are microcytic. The **Mentzer index** (MCV divided by red cell count) above 13 favors iron deficiency, because the marrow makes fewer cells; below 13 favors thalassemia trait, where the marrow makes many small cells.

**Physical clues**: pallor, **koilonychia** (spoon-shaped nails), angular cheilitis, glossitis, **pagophagia** (ice craving), and restless legs.

A crucial rule: IDA is a sign, not a diagnosis. In men and postmenopausal women, unexplained IDA demands a search for gastrointestinal bleeding, because it can be the first clue to colorectal or gastric cancer.
levels.phd:
Each iron study reflects a distinct biological compartment. **Serum ferritin** is secreted in proportion to tissue stores, so in healthy adults its concentration tracks total storage iron closely. **Transferrin** (TIBC) and **transferrin receptor 1 (TfR1)** rise because of the **IRP/IRE system**: in iron-poor cells, iron-regulatory proteins bind iron-responsive elements in mRNA. Binding to the 3' IREs of TfR1 mRNA stabilizes it, increasing receptor synthesis, while binding to the 5' IRE of ferritin mRNA blocks translation. Shed TfR1 circulates as **soluble transferrin receptor (sTfR)**, which rises with iron-deficient erythropoiesis and, unlike ferritin, is relatively unaffected by inflammation. The **sTfR/log ferritin index** exploits both.

Other markers capture the erythroid compartment directly. When iron is scarce, ferrochelatase inserts zinc into protoporphyrin IX, raising **zinc protoporphyrin**. **Reticulocyte hemoglobin content** (CHr or Ret-He) reports iron available to cells made over the previous few days, making it the earliest marker of iron-restricted erythropoiesis and of treatment response. Serum hepcidin is suppressed in true deficiency, maximizing absorption.

**Diagnostic accuracy and thresholds.** Guyatt's 1992 meta-analysis against marrow iron showed ferritin outperforms all other single tests, with very high likelihood ratios at low values. The problem is sensitivity: a cutoff of 15 ng/mL is highly specific but misses many cases. WHO's 2020 guideline uses ferritin below 15 ng/mL in healthy individuals aged five and over (below 12 in younger children), raised to below 70 (or 30 in young children) with infection or inflammation. The 2020 AGA guideline proposed 45 ng/mL. These differing cutoffs remain contested.

**Neurobiology.** Iron is a cofactor for **tyrosine hydroxylase** (dopamine synthesis) and is needed by oligodendrocytes for myelination. Lozoff's longitudinal cohorts found that infants with severe chronic iron deficiency had cognitive and motor differences persisting years after correction. Low brain iron in the substantia nigra, shown on MRI and autopsy, links iron deficiency to restless legs syndrome.

The historical gold standard, a bone marrow aspirate stained with **Prussian blue** (Perls stain), is now rarely needed.
levels.expert:
Clinically, the hard part is rarely confirming IDA; it is finding the cause and avoiding interpretive traps.

**Etiology workup.** In men and postmenopausal women, guidelines recommend bidirectional endoscopy, celiac serology, and testing for *H. pylori*. Autoimmune atrophic gastritis is increasingly recognized as a cause of oral iron failure. If endoscopies are negative and deficiency recurs, capsule endoscopy looks for small bowel angiodysplasia or tumors. In premenopausal women, heavy menstrual bleeding is chronically under-asked; a substantial minority have an underlying bleeding disorder such as von Willebrand disease.

**Interpretive pitfalls.**
- Ferritin is an acute-phase reactant. With inflammation, liver disease or malignancy, a normal ferritin can hide deficiency. Ferritin below 100 ng/mL with transferrin saturation below 20% suggests deficiency in inflamed patients.
- Serum iron has diurnal variation and spikes after recent iron intake, distorting saturation.
- Iron deficiency lowers **HbA2**, so electrophoresis done while iron-deficient can miss beta-thalassemia trait. Repeat after repletion.

**Heart failure controversy.** Trials such as FAIR-HF, AFFIRM-AHF and IRONMAN defined deficiency as ferritin below 100, or 100 to 299 with saturation below 20%. Grote Beverborg and colleagues (2018) found this definition matched marrow iron poorly; saturation of about 20% or less, or low serum iron, performed better.

**Treatment nuances (no doses here).** An oral iron dose raises hepcidin for about a day, so Stoffel's work suggests less frequent scheduling can improve fractional absorption and tolerability. IV formulations bypass hepcidin. **Ferric carboxymaltose** raises intact **FGF23**, causing renal phosphate wasting; the PHOSPHARE trials showed far more hypophosphatemia than with ferric derisomaltose, occasionally causing osteomalacia with repeated courses.

**IRIDA.** Lifelong microcytic anemia unresponsive to oral iron, with inappropriately normal or high hepcidin, suggests iron-refractory iron deficiency anemia from loss-of-function **TMPRSS6** variants.

**Surgical relevance.** Preoperative anemia predicts transfusion and complications in neurosurgery and elsewhere, driving patient blood management programs. Yet PREVENTT (Lancet 2020) found preoperative IV iron did not reduce transfusion or death after major abdominal surgery, though readmissions fell. Whether to treat iron deficiency without anemia remains open.

Main causes: blood loss, increased demand, poor intake or absorption
Classic pattern: low ferritin, low serum iron, high TIBC, low transferrin saturation
Ferritin is the most specific test but rises with inflammation
Cells are microcytic and hypochromic with high RDW; Mentzer index helps separate thalassemia trait
Unexplained IDA in men and postmenopausal women needs a GI bleeding workup

test.q: In an adult man with new iron deficiency anemia, which cause is most important to investigate?
test.explain: In men and postmenopausal women, IDA is usually from blood loss, often gastrointestinal, and can be the first sign of colorectal or gastric cancer. Vitamin C actually helps iron absorption.

test.q: Which single blood test is most specific for low body iron stores?
test.explain: Ferritin reflects stored iron, and a low ferritin is the most specific single marker. Serum iron fluctuates with time of day and recent meals.

test.q: Which pattern of iron studies fits iron deficiency?
choices: Low ferritin, low TIBC, high saturation
Low ferritin, high TIBC, low saturation
High ferritin, low TIBC, low saturation
High ferritin, high TIBC, high saturation
test.explain: Stores are empty (low ferritin), the body makes more transferrin (high TIBC), and transferrin carries little iron (low saturation).

test.q: The classic red cell appearance in established iron deficiency anemia is:
test.explain: Without enough iron, cells make less hemoglobin, so they are small (microcytic) and pale (hypochromic).

test.q: Because ferritin is an acute-phase reactant, in a patient with inflammation it can be:
test.explain: Inflammation raises ferritin, so a normal value can mask true iron deficiency. It does not falsely lower it.

test.q: Craving and chewing ice, a fairly specific symptom of iron deficiency, is called:
test.explain: Pagophagia is ice craving, a form of pica. Koilonychia is spoon nails, and glossitis and cheilitis affect the tongue and mouth corners.

test.q: A microcytic patient has a high red cell count, a normal RDW and a Mentzer index below 13. Which is more likely?
test.explain: A Mentzer index below 13 means many small cells, typical of thalassemia trait. Iron deficiency lowers cell count, pushing the index above 13.

test.q: Which group has higher iron needs mainly because of growing demand rather than loss?
test.explain: Pregnancy increases iron demand for the expanding blood volume and the fetus. The other groups lose iron through bleeding.

test.q: As iron deficiency develops, which change usually appears first?
test.explain: Iron depletion comes first: stores (ferritin) drop while hemoglobin is still normal. Anemia and microcytosis come later.

test.q: What term describes the spoon-shaped nails seen in chronic iron deficiency?
test.explain: Koilonychia means spoon-shaped, concave nails, a physical sign of long-standing iron deficiency.

test.q: Transferrin ___, calculated from serum iron and TIBC, is low in iron deficiency.
test.explain: Transferrin saturation shows how full the iron transport protein is; it falls when iron supply is short.

test.q: Which stain of a bone marrow aspirate is the historical gold standard for judging iron stores?
test.explain: Prussian blue (Perls) staining shows stored iron in the marrow, though blood tests have largely replaced it.

kidTest.q: What does iron help red blood cells do?
kidTest.explain: Iron lets red blood cells grab oxygen and carry it around the body.

kidTest.q: Which food has lots of iron?
kidTest.explain: Red meat, beans and spinach are iron-rich foods.

kidTest.q: How might a kid with very low iron feel?
kidTest.explain: Without enough iron, fewer oxygen trucks are made, so people feel tired and look pale.

kidTest.q: Losing blood can lower your iron because blood has:
kidTest.explain: Blood is full of iron, so losing blood means losing iron.

kidTest.q: Iron is stored in a box-like protein called f _ _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Ferritin is the iron storage box, and doctors measure it to see how much iron is stored.

advancedTest.q: A patient with active rheumatoid arthritis has microcytic anemia, ferritin of 80 ng/mL and transferrin saturation of 12%. Best interpretation?
choices: Hemochromatosis is suggested by the low saturation
Iron deficiency is likely despite this ferritin
Iron stores are clearly adequate given ferritin
The low saturation indicates thalassemia trait
advancedTest.explain: Inflammation raises ferritin, so in inflamed patients a ferritin below 100 with saturation below 20% suggests true iron deficiency. Hemochromatosis gives high saturation.

advancedTest.q: A microcytic, iron-deficient woman has normal HbA2 on electrophoresis. After iron repletion, microcytosis persists and repeat HbA2 is elevated. Best explanation?
choices: Iron deficiency had masked beta-thalassemia trait
Iron overload artificially raises HbA2 on retesting
Iron therapy triggered a new beta-globin mutation
The first test was contaminated by fetal hemoglobin
advancedTest.explain: Iron deficiency lowers HbA2, which can hide beta-thalassemia trait. Electrophoresis should be repeated once iron is replete.

advancedTest.q: Weeks after IV ferric carboxymaltose, a patient has muscle weakness and very low serum phosphate. The most likely mechanism is:
choices: Iron binds dietary phosphate, blocking its absorption
Iron deposits damage the parathyroid glands
New red cells rapidly consume serum phosphate
Raised intact FGF23 causes renal phosphate wasting
advancedTest.explain: Ferric carboxymaltose increases intact FGF23, which makes the kidneys excrete phosphate. PHOSPHARE showed this is much more common than with ferric derisomaltose.

advancedTest.q: A young adult has lifelong microcytic anemia, low ferritin, no response to oral iron, normal endoscopies, negative celiac serology and inappropriately high hepcidin. Most likely cause?
advancedTest.explain: IRIDA results from TMPRSS6 loss of function, leaving hepcidin inappropriately high and blocking gut iron absorption. HFE and ferroportin variants cause iron overload, not deficiency.

lessons.title: Anemia of Inflammation & Chronic Disease

levels.kid:
Germs need iron to grow, just like you need food. So when you get sick, your body plays a clever trick. It **hides its iron** where germs can't reach it, like locking the cookie jar on a high shelf.

A messenger from the liver called **hepcidin** shouts, "Lock up the iron!" Iron gets stuck inside special cleaner cells and stops coming in from your food.

The problem is that your **bone marrow**, the factory inside your bones that makes red blood cells, also needs that iron. With less iron, the factory slows down. Fewer red blood cells means less oxygen gets carried around, so a person can feel tired.

The best fix is to treat the sickness underneath. Then the iron gets unlocked again.
levels.hs:
**Anemia of inflammation**, also called **anemia of chronic disease (ACD)**, is anemia caused by long-lasting inflammation. It is the second most common anemia worldwide after iron deficiency, and the most common one in hospitalized patients.

Common causes:
- Chronic infections, such as tuberculosis or HIV
- Autoimmune diseases, such as rheumatoid arthritis or inflammatory bowel disease
- Cancer
- Chronic kidney disease and heart failure

The key player is **hepcidin**, a hormone made by the liver. Inflammation, especially the immune signal **interleukin-6 (IL-6)**, makes the liver release more hepcidin. Hepcidin blocks **ferroportin**, the only known protein that lets iron leave cells. Iron gets trapped inside macrophages and gut cells, so blood iron falls even though the body still has plenty stored. This is called **nutritional immunity**: starving microbes of the iron they need.

Inflammation also lowers production of **erythropoietin (EPO)**, the kidney hormone that tells bone marrow to make red cells, and makes the marrow respond weakly to it.

The anemia is usually mild to moderate, and red cells are usually normal in size (**normocytic**). Blood tests show low serum iron, but **ferritin** (the iron-storage protein) is normal or high. That separates it from iron deficiency, where ferritin is low. Example: a woman with active rheumatoid arthritis has low hemoglobin, low iron and a high ferritin. Her anemia usually improves when the arthritis is controlled. Iron pills often work poorly because hepcidin blocks absorption in the gut.
levels.college:
Anemia of inflammation (AI/ACD) is an **iron-restricted erythropoiesis**: total body iron is adequate, but iron is withheld from the marrow.

**Three mechanisms**
- **Iron sequestration.** IL-6 induces hepatic **hepcidin**, which binds **ferroportin** and causes it to be internalized and degraded. Macrophages that recycle iron from old red cells can't release it, and duodenal enterocytes can't export dietary iron. Serum iron falls within hours of an inflammatory insult.
- **Blunted erythropoietin.** IL-1 and TNF-alpha suppress renal EPO production, so EPO levels are lower than expected for the degree of anemia.
- **Suppressed, shortened erythropoiesis.** TNF-alpha, IL-1 and interferon-gamma inhibit erythroid progenitors. Activated macrophages also clear red cells faster, modestly shortening their lifespan.

**Lab pattern versus iron deficiency anemia (IDA)**
- Serum iron: low in both
- Transferrin (TIBC): normal or low in AI; high in IDA
- Transferrin saturation: low in both
- **Ferritin**: normal or high in AI, because it is an **acute-phase reactant**; low in IDA
- **Soluble transferrin receptor (sTfR)**: normal in AI; high in IDA, because iron-starved erythroblasts shed more receptor
- Zinc protoporphyrin rises in both, so it doesn't separate them

The anemia is usually **normocytic, normochromic**, and rarely falls below about 8 g/dL. Long-standing cases can become mildly microcytic, which can mimic IDA or thalassemia trait. Reticulocytes are low for the degree of anemia.

**Mixed disease is common.** A patient with inflammatory bowel disease may lose blood from the gut and have inflammation at the same time. Because inflammation raises ferritin, a 'normal' ferritin can hide real iron deficiency.

**Treatment**
- Treat the underlying disease, which is the most effective step.
- Oral iron is poorly absorbed while hepcidin is high. Intravenous iron bypasses the gut block.
- **Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESAs)** are used in selected settings such as CKD and chemotherapy-related anemia.
- Transfusion is reserved for severe or symptomatic anemia.
levels.phd:
Hepcidin, a 25-amino-acid peptide encoded by **HAMP**, is the hinge of AI. Its causal role was shown by three converging lines of work. Nicolas et al. (2002) found that mice overexpressing hepcidin develop severe iron-deficient anemia. Weinstein et al. (2002) described hepatic adenomas in glycogen storage disease that secreted hepcidin and caused iron-refractory anemia, which resolved after resection. Nemeth et al. (2004) showed that IL-6 is required for hepcidin induction during inflammation, and that IL-6 infusion in humans raised urinary hepcidin and dropped serum iron within hours.

**Signaling.** IL-6 binds its receptor and activates **JAK1/2-STAT3**. Phosphorylated STAT3 binds a STAT3 element in the HAMP promoter. Full induction also requires intact **BMP6-SMAD1/5/8-SMAD4** signaling, the same axis that tracks iron stores. Activin B and IL-1 contribute in some models. Hepcidin binds ferroportin, occluding its central iron channel and triggering ubiquitination, endocytosis and lysosomal degradation.

**Hepcidin-independent iron effects.** Interferon-gamma and LPS upregulate DMT1 and downregulate ferroportin transcription in macrophages. IL-10 increases transferrin receptor and ferritin expression, enhancing macrophage iron uptake and retention.

**Erythroid suppression.** IL-1 and TNF-alpha inhibit EPO gene transcription through NF-kB and GATA2 activity. Interferon-gamma reduces EPO receptor expression on CFU-E and promotes erythroid apoptosis. Red cell lifespan falls through macrophage activation and erythrophagocytosis.

**Counter-regulation.** Erythroblasts stimulated by EPO secrete **erythroferrone** (Kautz et al., 2014), which suppresses hepcidin by sequestering BMP ligands. Inflammation can outcompete this signal, which helps explain why EPO alone partly corrects AI.

**Adaptive or maladaptive?** Hypoferremia limits iron for siderophore-producing bacteria and intracellular pathogens, which is the nutritional immunity hypothesis. Supporting this, the 2006 Pemba trial of iron and folic acid in a malaria-endemic area found increased hospitalization and death in supplemented children. In sterile chronic inflammation, such as rheumatoid arthritis or CKD, the same response may simply cause harm. In CKD, reduced renal clearance of hepcidin adds to the inflammatory rise.
levels.expert:
**Diagnosis in practice.** No single test defines AI. A pragmatic approach pairs iron indices with CRP:
- Ferritin under 30 ng/mL indicates iron deficiency regardless of inflammation.
- With inflammation, ferritin under 100 ng/mL, or 100 to 300 ng/mL with transferrin saturation under 20%, suggests coexisting iron deficiency. CKD and heart failure guidelines use these cutoffs.
- The **sTfR/log ferritin index** helps: values under 1 favor pure AI, and values over 2 suggest added absolute iron deficiency.
- Reticulocyte hemoglobin content (CHr or Ret-He) falls in both conditions. It is useful for real-time iron-restricted erythropoiesis, but it doesn't separate the causes.
- A bone marrow iron stain was the historical gold standard and is now rarely needed. A response to IV iron often serves as the practical diagnostic test.

**Pitfalls.** Ferritin is also raised by liver disease, alcohol use and malignancy. Serum hepcidin assays remain poorly standardized and aren't routine. Anemia in critically ill patients is compounded by blood drawn for tests. Many cases of 'unexplained anemia of the elderly' show low-grade inflammation and relative EPO deficiency.

**Therapeutics**
- **Disease control lowers hepcidin.** Tocilizumab, an IL-6 receptor antibody, rapidly lowers hepcidin and raises hemoglobin in rheumatoid arthritis.
- **IV iron.** In heart failure with iron deficiency, FAIR-HF, AFFIRM-AHF and IRONMAN support IV iron for symptoms and hospitalization outcomes. Ferric carboxymaltose can cause FGF23-mediated hypophosphatemia, a frequently missed adverse effect.
- **ESAs.** TREAT (darbepoetin in diabetic CKD) found roughly doubled stroke risk, and CHOIR found harm with higher hemoglobin targets. ESAs now aim for partial correction, not normal hemoglobin. In cancer they carry concerns about tumor progression.
- **HIF prolyl hydroxylase inhibitors** raise endogenous EPO and lower hepcidin while upregulating iron-uptake genes. Daprodustat (2023) and vadadustat (2024) are FDA-approved for dialysis patients. Roxadustat is approved elsewhere but was not approved by the FDA.
- **Hepcidin-axis drugs.** Momelotinib, approved in 2023 for myelofibrosis, inhibits ACVR1/ALK2, lowers hepcidin and improves anemia. This is clinical proof that targeting the axis works.

**Open questions.** Does correcting AI improve outcomes beyond symptoms? Does IV iron raise infection risk in active infection? And which patients truly benefit from overriding a host-defense response?

IL-6 raises hepcidin, which degrades ferroportin and traps iron in macrophages and gut cells
Inflammation also blunts EPO production and suppresses erythroid progenitors
Typical labs: low iron, low or normal transferrin, normal or high ferritin, normal sTfR
Usually mild and normocytic; coexisting iron deficiency is common and easily missed
Treat the underlying disease; IV iron, ESAs or HIF-PH inhibitors in selected cases

choices: Iron overload with tissue iron deposition
Anemia of inflammation with full iron stores

advancedTest.q: Tocilizumab improves hemoglobin in rheumatoid arthritis mainly by:

advancedTest.q: Besides raising endogenous EPO, why do HIF prolyl hydroxylase inhibitors improve iron availability?

They prevent transferrin from binding plasma iron
They increase hepatic ferritin synthesis and storage
They lower hepcidin and raise iron-uptake genes

Raise hemoglobin partway, not to normal

lessons.title: Iron Overload & Hereditary Hemochromatosis

levels.kid:
Your body needs iron to build red blood cells, the tiny trucks that carry oxygen everywhere. But here is a strange fact: your body has almost no way to get rid of extra iron. So it is very careful about how much it lets in from food.

The body has a gatekeeper called **hepcidin**. When you already have enough iron, hepcidin closes the gate. In a condition called **hemochromatosis**, the gatekeeper is too weak. The gate stays open, and iron slowly piles up for years, like junk filling a garage.

Too much iron can harm the liver, the heart and the joints. The fix is surprisingly simple. Doctors take out some blood every so often. Each time, the body uses its stored iron to make new blood, and the extra iron goes away.
levels.hs:
**Iron overload** means the body has stored far more iron than it needs. This matters because humans have **no regulated way to excrete iron**. We lose only small amounts through shed skin and gut cells and through bleeding. Balance depends almost entirely on controlling how much iron the gut absorbs.

That control comes from **hepcidin**, a hormone made by the liver. In **hereditary hemochromatosis (HH)**, a genetic change keeps hepcidin too low, so the gut keeps absorbing iron even when stores are full.

Key facts:
- The most common cause is two copies of the **C282Y** variant in the **HFE** gene. About 1 in 200 to 300 people of Northern European ancestry have this.
- Iron builds up over decades. Men usually show problems in their 40s to 60s. Women present later because **menstruation and pregnancy** remove iron.
- Excess iron damages the liver (scarring, called cirrhosis), pancreas (diabetes), heart, joints and skin. Darker skin plus diabetes was once called **"bronze diabetes."**
- Screening blood tests are **transferrin saturation** (how full the iron-carrying protein is) and **ferritin** (the iron-storage protein).

Example: a 52-year-old man has tiredness, aching knuckles and new diabetes. His transferrin saturation and ferritin are high, and genetic testing shows C282Y on both copies of HFE.

Treatment is **therapeutic phlebotomy**: regularly removing blood, like a blood donation. Iron overload can also be **secondary**, for example from repeated transfusions.
levels.college:
Iron overload occurs when intake exceeds losses for years. Because there is no regulated excretion pathway, the only controllable step is entry, governed by the **hepcidin-ferroportin axis**. Hepcidin binds the iron exporter **ferroportin** on duodenal enterocytes and macrophages and causes it to be internalized and degraded. Low hepcidin leaves ferroportin active, which increases absorption and releases recycled iron from macrophages.

**Primary (hereditary) hemochromatosis** comes from inappropriately low hepcidin, or from ferroportin that resists hepcidin:
- **Type 1, HFE**: C282Y homozygosity, adult onset, by far the most common form.
- **Type 2 (juvenile)**: hemojuvelin (HJV, type 2A) or HAMP, the hepcidin gene itself (type 2B). Severe, with cardiomyopathy and hypogonadism before age 30.
- **Type 3, TFR2**: intermediate severity.
- **Type 4, ferroportin disease (SLC40A1)**: autosomal dominant, unlike the recessive types 1 to 3.

**Secondary iron overload** follows chronic transfusion (thalassemia major, myelodysplastic syndromes, sickle cell disease) or ineffective erythropoiesis, which suppresses hepcidin even without transfusion.

**Why iron is toxic.** When transferrin saturation rises (roughly above 75%), **non-transferrin-bound iron (NTBI)** appears in plasma and enters hepatocytes, cardiomyocytes and endocrine cells without normal regulation. Free iron catalyzes the **Fenton reaction**, producing hydroxyl radicals. These cause lipid peroxidation, mitochondrial damage and fibrosis.

**Clinical features**: fatigue, arthropathy of the **second and third metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints**, skin bronzing, elevated liver enzymes, cirrhosis, **hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC)**, diabetes, cardiomyopathy and arrhythmias, and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism from pituitary iron.

**Diagnosis**: fasting transferrin saturation above about 45% plus raised ferritin leads to HFE genotyping. MRI can quantify liver and heart iron.

**Treatment**: phlebotomy for HH. **Iron chelators** (deferoxamine, deferasirox, deferiprone) are used for transfusional overload, where removing blood is not an option.
levels.phd:
**HFE biology.** HFE was identified by positional cloning (Feder et al., 1996). It encodes an MHC class I-like protein that pairs with **beta2-microglobulin**. C282Y destroys a disulfide bond in the alpha3 domain, so the mutant protein cannot bind beta2-microglobulin, stays trapped in the endoplasmic reticulum, and never reaches the cell surface. In hepatocytes, HFE normally competes with diferric transferrin for **TfR1**. When saturation rises, HFE is displaced toward **TFR2**, and the complex amplifies **BMP6-driven signaling** through the BMP receptor, the co-receptor **hemojuvelin**, and **SMAD1/5/8-SMAD4**, which transcribes HAMP. Losing HFE, TFR2 or HJV blunts this iron-sensing signal. Hepcidin is then too low for the body's iron load. HJV and HAMP mutations cut the pathway more severely, which explains the juvenile phenotype.

**Ferroportin disease** shows a genotype-phenotype split:
- **Loss-of-function (type 4A)**: iron is trapped in macrophages (Kupffer cells, spleen). Ferritin is high but transferrin saturation is normal or low, and patients may tolerate phlebotomy poorly.
- **Gain-of-function, hepcidin-resistant (type 4B)**: mimics classic HH, with high saturation and parenchymal loading.

**Erythroid regulation.** Erythroblasts secrete **erythroferrone (ERFE)**, which sequesters BMP ligands and suppresses hepcidin. In non-transfusion-dependent thalassemia, the expanded ineffective erythroid mass drives absorption and causes overload with no transfusions at all.

**Uptake of NTBI.** NTBI and its redox-active fraction, labile plasma iron, enter cells through **ZIP14** (SLC39A14) in liver and pancreas and possibly through L-type and T-type calcium channels in cardiomyocytes. This explains why heart and endocrine loading follow saturation more closely than total stores.

**Penetrance.** Biochemical expression of C282Y homozygosity is common, but clinical disease is not. In the Melbourne cohort (Allen et al., NEJM 2008), documented iron-overload-related disease occurred in about 28% of male and about 1% of female homozygotes. Modifiers include sex, blood loss, alcohol, metabolic liver disease and variants in other iron genes. More recently, UK Biobank data (Pilling et al., 2019) found more liver disease, arthritis, diabetes and higher mortality in homozygous men, and more morbidity in women than earlier estimates suggested. This reopened the debate over how "low" penetrance really is.
levels.expert:
**Interpreting high ferritin is the main pitfall.** Most hyperferritinemia is *not* iron overload. Ferritin is an acute-phase reactant and also rises with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, alcohol, hepatocellular injury, malignancy and hemophagocytic syndromes. Transferrin saturation is the discriminator. High ferritin with normal saturation points to inflammation or metabolic causes, or to rare entities: loss-of-function ferroportin disease, **hereditary hyperferritinemia-cataract syndrome** (L-ferritin IRE mutations, no iron overload), and **aceruloplasminemia**. Aceruloplasminemia is relevant to neurology because it combines diabetes, retinal degeneration and brain iron deposition with movement disorders and dementia.

**Staging.** In C282Y homozygotes, a serum ferritin in the thousands together with raised transaminases marks substantial cirrhosis risk. Fibrosis should be assessed with elastography, or biopsy if results are unclear. Liver iron is quantified non-invasively with MRI **R2\* or R2 (FerriScan)**. **Cardiac T2\*** below 20 ms indicates myocardial iron, and below 10 ms predicts heart failure risk in transfusional overload. Established cirrhosis requires lifelong **HCC surveillance**, typically ultrasound every 6 months, because cancer risk persists after iron depletion.

**Management nuances.**
- Phlebotomy induction aims to bring ferritin down into the low-normal range while monitoring hemoglobin, followed by individualized maintenance. **Erythrocytapheresis** removes more red cell mass per session.
- Fatigue, skin pigmentation and transaminases improve. Arthropathy, hypogonadism and established cirrhosis often do not. This is the main argument for early detection.
- Advise against iron and vitamin C supplements and raw shellfish (**Vibrio vulnificus**, which thrives on iron), and limit alcohol.
- Chelators carry specific risks: agranulocytosis with deferiprone, renal and hepatic toxicity with deferasirox, and auditory or ocular toxicity with deferoxamine.

**Screening.** Population screening is not recommended because of incomplete penetrance. **Cascade testing of first-degree relatives** is standard. In many jurisdictions, blood removed from HH patients can be accepted as donor blood.

**Frontiers.** Hepcidin-pathway drugs aim to fix the root defect: hepcidin mimetics (rusfertide, positive phase 3 data in polycythemia vera, also studied in HH), **TMPRSS6** silencing to raise endogenous hepcidin, and oral ferroportin inhibitors (vamifeport). In thalassemia, luspatercept lowers transfusion burden and so reduces iron intake. Open questions include whether early treatment of asymptomatic women homozygotes changes outcomes, and how to treat iron loading caused by ineffective erythropoiesis.

keyPoints: The body has no regulated iron excretion, so balance depends on absorption
Hereditary hemochromatosis comes from inappropriately low hepcidin, most often HFE C282Y homozygosity
Free iron (NTBI) damages liver, heart, pancreas, joints and pituitary via Fenton chemistry
Screen with transferrin saturation plus ferritin, then genotype HFE
Phlebotomy treats HH; chelation treats transfusional overload
High ferritin with normal transferrin saturation is usually not iron overload

test.explain: Hepcidin degrades ferroportin. Too little hepcidin lets iron flow in unchecked.

test.explain: Iron and melanin darken the skin, and pancreatic iron causes diabetes, hence 'bronze diabetes.'

kidTest.explain: Hepcidin closes the gate when you have enough iron.

kidTest.explain: Iron builds up in hemochromatosis because the body has almost no way to remove it.

lessons.title: Vitamin B12, Folate & Megaloblastic Anemia

levels.kid:
Your body makes millions of new red blood cells every second. To build each one, a cell has to copy its instruction book, called DNA, before it splits in two.

Copying DNA needs two helper vitamins: **vitamin B12** and **folate**. Folate comes from leafy green vegetables. B12 comes from foods like meat, eggs, fish and milk.

If a helper is missing, the cells keep growing but can't finish copying their book. So they get too big and clumsy, and not enough of them are made. Doctors call this **megaloblastic anemia**. "Megalo" means big!

B12 also helps keep your nerves healthy, a bit like the plastic coating on a wire. That's why missing B12 can make hands and feet tingle.
levels.hs:
**Megaloblastic anemia** is anemia in which the marrow makes abnormally large red cell precursors (**megaloblasts**) because DNA synthesis is impaired while the cell's cytoplasm keeps growing. Blood tests show a high **MCV** (mean corpuscular volume, the average size of red cells), so these are **macrocytic** cells.

The two usual causes are deficiency of **folate** (vitamin B9) or **vitamin B12** (cobalamin). Both are needed to make thymidine, one of the DNA building blocks.

- **Folate** is found in leafy greens, legumes and fortified grains. The body stores only a few months' worth, so poor diet, alcohol use disorder, pregnancy and some medicines (like methotrexate) can quickly cause deficiency.
- **Vitamin B12** comes only from animal foods. The liver stores several years' worth. Absorbing it requires **intrinsic factor**, a protein made by the stomach.

A classic example is **pernicious anemia**, an autoimmune disease in which the immune system attacks the stomach cells that make intrinsic factor. Without intrinsic factor, B12 can't be absorbed even when the diet contains plenty.

A key difference: B12 deficiency can damage the nervous system, causing numbness, poor balance and memory problems. Folate deficiency does not. Giving folate alone to someone who actually lacks B12 can improve the blood count while nerve damage keeps progressing. That is why doctors check both vitamins.
levels.college:
**Shared biochemistry.** Folate, as 5,10-methylene-tetrahydrofolate (THF), donates a carbon to **thymidylate synthase**, which converts dUMP to dTMP. B12 links in through **methionine synthase**, which transfers a methyl group from 5-methyl-THF to homocysteine, making methionine and regenerating THF. Without B12, folate becomes trapped as 5-methyl-THF (the **methyl-folate trap**), producing a functional folate deficiency. In both cases dTMP falls and uracil is misincorporated into DNA. S-phase stalls while RNA and protein synthesis continue, causing **nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony**.

**Consequences.**
- Many megaloblasts die in the marrow (**ineffective erythropoiesis**). This raises LDH and indirect bilirubin.
- Blood: macro-ovalocytes, often MCV >100 fL; **hypersegmented neutrophils** (≥6 lobes, or more than 5% with 5 lobes); sometimes pancytopenia.
- Rapidly dividing epithelium is also affected, causing glossitis.

**B12 absorption pathway.** Haptocorrin (R-binder) in saliva binds B12 in the stomach. Pancreatic proteases free it in the duodenum, and it then binds **intrinsic factor** from gastric parietal cells. The IF-B12 complex is taken up by the **cubam receptor** in the terminal ileum. In plasma, **transcobalamin** delivers B12 to cells.

**Causes.**
- B12: pernicious anemia, gastrectomy or bariatric surgery, ileal resection or Crohn disease, strict vegan diet, metformin, long-term acid suppression, *Diphyllobothrium latum*, and nitrous oxide, which oxidizes cobalamin.
- Folate: poor diet, alcohol, pregnancy, hemolysis, and drugs such as methotrexate, trimethoprim and phenytoin.

**Neurology.** B12 is also a cofactor for **methylmalonyl-CoA mutase**. Deficiency causes **subacute combined degeneration** of the dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts, peripheral neuropathy and cognitive change.

**Labs.** Homocysteine rises in both deficiencies. **Methylmalonic acid (MMA)** rises only in B12 deficiency.
levels.phd:
Uracil misincorporation is the mechanistic core. When dTMP is scarce, the dUTP:dTTP ratio rises, and uracil-DNA glycosylase repeatedly excises uracil from DNA. Closely spaced repair gaps on opposite strands become double-strand breaks, and the cells undergo apoptosis. This futile repair cycle, rather than simple slowing of DNA synthesis, explains intramedullary cell death and the hemolysis-like lab picture: very high LDH, low haptoglobin and indirect hyperbilirubinemia. The deoxyuridine suppression test, historically used to separate B12 from folate defects, rests on this same biology.

The **methyl-folate trap** hypothesis (Herbert and Zalusky, 1962) arose from the observation that methyl-THF accumulates in serum during B12 deficiency. The reduction of 5,10-methylene-THF to 5-methyl-THF by MTHFR is essentially irreversible, so methionine synthase is the main exit route. This explains why pharmacological folic acid, which enters the cycle as dihydrofolate and bypasses the trap, can correct the hematology of B12 deficiency.

The neuropathology is less settled. Candidate mechanisms include:
- **Impaired methylation**: low S-adenosylmethionine reduces myelin basic protein methylation. Nitrous oxide inactivation of methionine synthase reproduces myelopathy, which supports this pathway.
- **Methylmalonyl-CoA accumulation**: abnormal odd-chain and branched-chain fatty acids may be incorporated into myelin.
- **Cytokine dysregulation**: altered TNF-α and EGF balance has been proposed, from rodent data.

Neurological and hematological damage can be dissociated. Up to roughly a quarter of patients with B12 neuropathy have no anemia or macrocytosis, especially when folate intake is high.

In pernicious anemia, autoimmune gastritis targets the parietal cell **H+/K+-ATPase**. Anti-IF antibodies are highly specific but only about 50-70% sensitive. Achlorhydria causes compensatory G-cell hyperplasia and hypergastrinemia, which raises the risk of gastric neuroendocrine tumors and adenocarcinoma.

Inherited disorders illustrate each step: Imerslund-Gräsbeck syndrome (mutations in CUBN or AMN, the cubam components), transcobalamin II deficiency, and cblC defects of intracellular cobalamin processing. Hereditary folate malabsorption is caused by mutations in PCFT (SLC46A1).
levels.expert:
**Diagnostic pitfalls.** Serum B12 assays are imperfect. Values in the low-normal range are a grey zone, and anti-IF antibodies can interfere with competitive-binding immunoassays, producing falsely normal results in pernicious anemia. Holotranscobalamin ('active B12') and MMA improve accuracy. MMA rises falsely in renal impairment, and homocysteine also rises with hypothyroidism and MTHFR variants. Serum folate reflects recent intake; red cell folate reflects stores better. In fortified populations, isolated folate deficiency is now uncommon.

**Macrocytosis is not always megaloblastic.** Alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism, reticulocytosis, and drugs such as hydroxyurea, azathioprine and antiretrovirals also raise MCV. A markedly raised MCV with cytopenias and no vitamin deficiency points toward **myelodysplastic syndrome**, which needs a marrow examination. Concurrent iron deficiency can mask macrocytosis; a high RDW is the clue.

**Treatment principles.** Replace B12 before or together with folate. Intramuscular B12 is traditional for pernicious anemia, but high-dose oral B12 works through passive, IF-independent diffusion and is a valid alternative. Reticulocytes peak around days 5-7. **Hypokalemia** can occur in severe cases as potassium shifts into newly forming cells. Neurological recovery depends on how long deficits have been present and may be incomplete, which is why early recognition matters.

**Neurosurgical relevance.** Nitrous oxide anesthesia can precipitate acute subacute combined degeneration in patients with unrecognized low B12. MRI shows an inverted-V T2 signal in the dorsal columns of the cervical cord, which can mimic compressive or demyelinating myelopathy. Checking B12, MMA and copper prevents unnecessary decompression. Copper deficiency, for example after bariatric surgery or with zinc excess, causes a near-identical myelopathy along with cytopenias.

**Severe presentations.** Profound deficiency can mimic thrombotic microangiopathy (**pseudo-TMA**), with schistocytes, very high LDH and low haptoglobin. A low reticulocyte count and very high LDH favor vitamin deficiency and can prevent unneeded plasma exchange.

**Open questions** include the optimal screening of patients on long-term metformin or proton-pump inhibitors, whether subclinical B12 deficiency contributes to cognitive decline in older adults, and how universal folic acid fortification, which cuts neural tube defects, affects masked B12 neuropathy at the population level.

keyPoints: B12 and folate are both needed to make thymidine for DNA synthesis
Impaired DNA synthesis with normal cytoplasmic growth produces large megaloblasts and a high MCV
Hypersegmented neutrophils and ineffective erythropoiesis (high LDH) are classic findings
B12 absorption needs intrinsic factor and the terminal ileum; pernicious anemia destroys intrinsic factor production
Only B12 deficiency causes neurological damage (subacute combined degeneration) and raised MMA
Folic acid alone can fix the blood count in B12 deficiency while nerve damage progresses

test.q: Why are red cell precursors abnormally large in megaloblastic anemia?
choices: Iron fails to enter the developing cell
DNA synthesis lags while cytoplasm keeps growing
The cell membrane loses its spectrin skeleton
test.explain: Nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony: S-phase stalls without enough thymidine, but RNA and protein synthesis continue, so the cell keeps enlarging.

test.q: Which lab result best distinguishes B12 deficiency from folate deficiency?
test.explain: MMA rises only when B12 is lacking, because B12 is the cofactor for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase. Homocysteine, MCV and LDH can rise in both deficiencies.

test.q: Where is the intrinsic factor-B12 complex absorbed?
test.explain: The cubam receptor in the terminal ileum takes up the IF-B12 complex. This is why ileal resection or Crohn disease causes B12 deficiency.

test.q: Pernicious anemia is caused by:
choices: Autoimmune loss of intrinsic factor production
Inherited failure to absorb dietary folate
A strict vegan diet lacking animal foods
A tapeworm absorbing dietary vitamin B12
test.explain: Autoimmune gastritis destroys parietal cells and blocks intrinsic factor. Diet and tapeworms are separate causes of B12 deficiency.

test.q: Which blood smear finding is classic for megaloblastic anemia?
test.explain: Impaired DNA synthesis also affects neutrophils, which develop six or more nuclear lobes.

test.q: Why does folate deficiency develop faster than B12 deficiency?
choices: Body folate stores last a few months
Folate requires a rare transport protein
Folate is destroyed by intrinsic factor
Folate is absorbed mainly in the stomach
test.explain: Folate stores last months, whereas the liver holds several years of B12.

test.q: Subacute combined degeneration affects which spinal cord regions?
choices: Ventral roots and dorsal root ganglia
Dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts
test.explain: B12 deficiency damages myelin in the dorsal columns (vibration and position sense) and the lateral corticospinal tracts (motor pathways).

test.q: What is the danger of giving folic acid alone to a B12-deficient patient?
choices: Anemia improves while nerve damage advances
test.explain: Folic acid bypasses the methyl-folate trap and corrects the blood count, but it does not fix the neurological pathway.

test.q: Why is LDH often high in megaloblastic anemia?
choices: Megaloblasts die within the bone marrow
The liver releases it in response to low folate
test.explain: Ineffective erythropoiesis: many megaloblasts die in the marrow and release LDH and bilirubin.

test.q: What stomach-made protein is required to absorb vitamin B12?
test.explain: Parietal cells secrete intrinsic factor, which binds B12 for uptake in the ileum.

test.q: Folate donates a carbon so thymidylate ___ can convert dUMP to dTMP.
test.explain: Thymidylate synthase makes dTMP, the thymidine nucleotide needed for DNA.

test.q: What is the chemical name for vitamin B12?
test.explain: B12 is called cobalamin because of the cobalt atom at its core.

kidTest.q: What do red blood cells look like in megaloblastic anemia?
kidTest.explain: "Megalo" means big. The cells grow but can't finish copying their DNA.

kidTest.q: Which food gives you folate?
kidTest.explain: Folate is found in leafy greens.

kidTest.q: Where does vitamin B12 come from?
kidTest.explain: B12 comes from foods like meat, eggs, fish and milk.

kidTest.q: Missing B12 can make hands and feet:
kidTest.explain: B12 protects nerves, so missing it can cause tingling.

kidTest.q: Cells must copy their instruction book before splitting. What is it called? D _ _
kidTest.explain: DNA is the cell's instruction book, and copying it needs B12 and folate.

advancedTest.q: Why does B12 deficiency produce a functional folate deficiency?
choices: B12 is needed to absorb folate across the ileum
B12 deficiency increases urinary loss of folate
Intrinsic factor antibodies bind folate in the plasma
Folate becomes trapped as 5-methyl-THF without methionine synthase
advancedTest.explain: MTHFR's reaction is essentially irreversible, so without B12-dependent methionine synthase, folate accumulates as methyl-THF and cannot regenerate THF.

advancedTest.q: A patient develops myelopathy after nitrous oxide anesthesia. Which finding best supports B12-related injury?
choices: Low MMA with a normal homocysteine
Raised anti-IF antibodies with a low MCV
Raised MMA and dorsal column T2 signal
advancedTest.explain: Nitrous oxide inactivates cobalamin. Raised MMA and the inverted-V dorsal column MRI signal fit subacute combined degeneration.

advancedTest.q: Severe B12 deficiency mimicking a thrombotic microangiopathy is suggested by:
choices: High reticulocyte count with modest LDH
Low reticulocyte count with very high LDH
advancedTest.explain: Intramedullary death produces very high LDH but few reticulocytes, unlike peripheral hemolysis, where the reticulocyte count rises.

advancedTest.q: Why does uracil misincorporation kill megaloblasts?
choices: It prevents iron from entering mitochondria
Repeated excision repair creates double-strand breaks
advancedTest.explain: Uracil-DNA glycosylase repeatedly excises uracil. Closely spaced repair gaps on opposite strands form double-strand breaks, triggering apoptosis.
